summary: Gives examples and ideas for how operators can use BGP Large Communities. It suggests logical categories and an orderly way to organize community values to achieve typical routing policy goals. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Network operators can stick labels on routes. This gives tips for keeping those labels tidy so they are easy to understand.

subtitle: Practical methods for organizing and using BGP Large Communities

tldr.problem: BGP Large Communities provide a way to label routes with metadata, but operators need guidance on how to organize and use these labels consistently.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes organizing communities as ASN:Function:Parameter, dividing them into Informational Communities (labels for attributes like origin and location) and Action Communities (requests to manipulate routing behavior).
tldr.outcome: Operators can now deploy structured community policies for traffic engineering, regional routing control, and route distribution management.

facts.label: Authors
facts.value: Job Snijders, John Heasley, Martijn Schmidt

today: RFC 8195 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It provides operational guidance for deploying BGP Large Communities in production networks and remains a key reference for network operators using this feature.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Overview
sections.content:
BGP Large Communities are an extension to BGP that allows operators to attach opaque metadata to routes. Unlike earlier BGP Communities, Large Communities have more space for values. The RFC proposes a standard structure: ASN:Function:Parameter, where the ASN is the Autonomous System that defines the meaning of the function and parameter.

The document draws on experience from operator communities like NANOG and NLNOG. It presents two categories of communities. Informational Communities are labels describing attributes such as route origin, location, or relationship type. Action Communities are requests to perform a specific routing action, such as filtering a route or changing its preference.
sections.eli5: You can write labels on routes. This says how to organize those labels in a way everyone can understand.

sections.title: Informational Communities: Labeling Routes
sections.content:
Informational Communities describe a route's attributes. The Global Administrator field is the ASN of the network adding the label. Function identifiers can represent location (using ISO 3166-1 country codes or UN M.49 region codes) or relationship (whether the route originated locally, came from a customer, peering partner, or transit provider).

For example, AS 64497 might use community 64497:1:528 to mark routes learned in the Netherlands, or 64497:2:150 to mark routes learned in Europe. Community 64497:3:2 indicates a customer-learned route. A single route may carry multiple Informational Communities. These labels assist downstream networks and the originating AS in understanding route characteristics for debugging and planning.
sections.eli5: Stick labels on routes saying where they came from, what region they are in, or what kind of network sent them. Anyone can read these labels to understand the route.

sections.title: Action Communities: Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
Action Communities are requests that a route be treated in a particular way. The Global Administrator is the ASN that performs the requested action. A customer might add a community with the provider's ASN requesting that the provider apply a specific routing policy.

The RFC gives examples: selective NO_EXPORT (prevent a route from being sent to specific neighbors), selective AS_PATH prepending (make a route less preferred to certain neighbors), manipulation of LOCAL_PREF (change the priority within an AS), and route server prefix distribution control. Each function gets a unique identifier. For instance, AS 64497 might use function 4 for ASN-based NO_EXPORT or function 5 for location-based NO_EXPORT. Operators should publicly document the functions they support and the order in which action communities are processed.
sections.eli5: Use labels to tell a router how to handle routes: "do not send to this neighbor," "make this route less popular," or "give this route lower priority."

sections.title: Practical Examples and Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates a four-AS topology and walks through real-world scenarios. A network operator can use informational communities to document that a route was learned in Japan (64497:1:392) or from a peering partner (64497:3:3). Operators can expose traffic-engineering functions to customers: AS 64497 might allow customer AS 64498 to mark routes with 64497:4:64499 to request that AS 64497 not advertise those routes to AS 64499.

Location-based functions work similarly: a community like 64497:5:840 tells AS 64497 not to export the route to neighbors in the United States. AS_PATH prepending functions are organized the same way. LOCAL_PREF manipulation functions assign preference classes (normal customer, backup customer, peering, upstream transit, fallback) and either apply them globally (with parameter 0) or regionally (with UN M.49 codes).

Route servers use a variant where function 0 blocks distribution and function 1 allows it, enabling clients to specify which peers to advertise to.
sections.eli5: A network operator in Japan wants their routes available in Europe but not the US. They add a community, and their provider filters accordingly. All done with labels.

sections.title: Security and Documentation
sections.content:
Operators should handle BGP Large Communities with the ASN in the Global Administrator field with care. Any community can be carried in a BGP UPDATE. Customers and downstream networks may use communities defined by other neighbors, and it is beneficial to permit this while being aware of the implications.

Operators are encouraged to publicly publish and maintain documentation on the purpose of each BGP Large Community they support or that is visible in their routing tables. This openness assists the broader network operator community and reduces operational confusion.
sections.eli5: Be careful who can put labels on your routes. Tell everyone what your labels mean so other operators know how to use them.

sections.title: Deployment and Integration
sections.content:
The opaque nature of BGP Large Communities allows rapid deployment of new features and routing policy changes. Because the meaning is determined by the operator, new functions can be introduced without protocol changes. Integration with existing BGP Community practices is straightforward: many operators already use standard communities (RFC 1997) for similar purposes, and Large Communities extend this practice to more complex scenarios.

The RFC notes that the same principles apply whether you use communities for simple operations or complex traffic engineering. The key is consistent documentation and clear communication of how functions are processed in routing policies.
sections.eli5: Once operators agree on what a label means, they can start using it. Adding new kinds of labels is fast and does not require changing BGP itself.
